lessons.title: Evaluating an argument
lessons.description: Separate a writer's claim from reasons and evidence, then judge whether the support is relevant.
lessons.content: An argument presents a claim and supports it with reasons and evidence. A claim is the position being defended. Evidence may include examples, observations or reliable data. A strong argument connects relevant evidence to its claim and acknowledges important limits.
learning_objectives: Identify a claim, reason and supporting evidence.
Assess whether evidence is relevant to a claim.
prerequisites: Read informational paragraphs and identify their main ideas.

explanation_sections.title: Trace the reasoning
explanation_sections.body: Ask what the writer wants readers to accept, why they should accept it, and what proof is offered. A statement that merely repeats the claim is not independent evidence.

explanation_sections.title: Check the strength
explanation_sections.body: Relevant evidence addresses the claim. One personal example can illustrate a point but may not prove a rule for everyone. Look for fair treatment of counterarguments and avoid confusing correlation with cause.

worked_examples.prompt: Claim: 'The school should provide shaded study areas.' Evidence: 'Learners report that the open courtyard is too hot at midday.' What is the link?
worked_examples.solution: The report gives a reason to consider shade because it identifies discomfort in the current study area.
worked_examples.reasoning: The evidence relates to comfort but a careful argument would also consider cost, safety and how many learners are affected.

lessons.author: ElimuQuest Curriculum Team

questions.prompt: Which part of an argument states the position the writer wants readers to accept?
questions.explanation: The claim is the position supported by the argument's reasons and evidence.

questions.prompt: A writer claims that a new library schedule improves access. Which evidence is most relevant?
options: Records show more learners borrowed books during the new opening hours.
The library walls were painted last year.
One learner likes the colour of the library sign.
The writer's favourite subject is English.
questions.correct_answer: Records show more learners borrowed books during the new opening hours.
questions.explanation: Borrowing records during the new hours directly relate to access.

questions.prompt: Why might one person's experience be insufficient to prove that a rule works for everyone?
options: One example may not represent all people or situations.
Personal experiences can never be useful.
questions.correct_answer: One example may not represent all people or situations.
questions.explanation: An example can illustrate an idea, but broader claims need evidence that is representative and relevant.

lessons.title: Formal register in writing
lessons.description: Choose language and organisation suitable for a formal letter or report.
lessons.content: Register is the level and style of language chosen for a purpose and audience. Formal writing uses respectful wording, complete sentences and a clear structure. It avoids slang and unexplained abbreviations.
learning_objectives: Organise a formal request with a clear purpose.
Edit informal wording for a formal audience.

explanation_sections.title: Audience and purpose
explanation_sections.body: Before writing, identify the reader and what you want them to understand or do. A formal request should state its purpose early, use courteous language and include relevant facts.

explanation_sections.title: Edit for clarity
explanation_sections.body: Replace slang with precise words, check subject–verb agreement, and divide long paragraphs. Use a suitable greeting and closing for the recipient and context.

worked_examples.prompt: Revise 'Hey, send me the timetable quick' for a formal email to a school office.
worked_examples.solution: Dear Sir or Madam, could you please send me the current timetable when convenient? Thank you.
worked_examples.reasoning: The revision uses a respectful greeting, a clear request and a courteous closing.

lessons.author: ElimuQuest Curriculum Team

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a suitable formal register for a letter to a school office?
options: I would be grateful if you could provide the meeting date.
questions.correct_answer: I would be grateful if you could provide the meeting date.
questions.explanation: It is courteous, precise and appropriate for a formal request.

questions.prompt: What should a formal request usually make clear near the beginning?
questions.explanation: Stating the purpose early helps the recipient understand the request.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence with correct subject–verb agreement.
options: The list of participants is attached.
The list of participants are attached.
The list of participants be attached.
The list of participants were attach.
questions.correct_answer: The list of participants is attached.
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular noun list, so the verb is is.
